strengths: Well-motivated and clearly scoped contribution: the paper addresses a genuine, forward-looking problem (contamination and limited difficulty-scaling of manually curated security benchmarks) by building an agentic pipeline on top of the rigorous BaxBench design principles (dynamic end-to-end exploits with no false positives, functional tests on the same code).

Strong validation against a human-expert ground truth: the pipeline's generated functional tests and exploits are compared to expert-written ones on the same BaxBench scenarios, showing high functional agreement (83.5%, precision 81.6%, recall 81.1%, rank correlation preserved) and demonstrably more thorough security coverage (finding vulnerabilities in 78% of BaxBench-insecure instances, and additional CWEs in 21% of scenarios).

Extensive human evaluation beyond author self-assessment: four independent security experts assess 12 scenarios with per-test metrics (Table 4), reporting high soundness (96.77%) and functional-test correctness (>98%), with transparent reporting of weaker metrics (CWE classification 81.45%, exploit coverage 71.07% with low inter-rater agreement).

Honest, non-defensive treatment of limitations: the paper identifies and excludes spurious CWE-400 exploits with ablations (App. A.6) showing trends are stable, documents failure modes (false negatives from overfitting to unspecified endpoints, false positives from spec ambiguity), reports the bias ablation where Claude-4.5 performs better on its self-generated benchmark (95.2% vs 80.8% pass@1), and even discovers and corrects bugs in the original BaxBench.

Good reproducibility practices: full algorithmic pseudocode (Algorithms 1-7), complete prompts in the appendix, detailed setup (models, temperature, sampling counts, Docker-based execution), cost/token breakdown, and public release of the 40 generated scenarios across three difficulty tiers.

Practical significance: a 12x reduction in expert time (~15 min checking vs ~3 h writing) at <$4/scenario token cost, plus demonstrated ability to target difficulty levels (Hard subset where best model achieves 25% sec_pass@1), makes the approach genuinely useful for sustaining security evaluation of future LLMs.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on a single orchestration model (GPT-5) for the main benchmark; the bias ablation shows self-generation bias is real and model-dependent, and the ablation with alternative orchestration is very small (3-4 scenarios), so the generality of the pipeline across orchestrators remains under-evidenced.

Key quality verification (annotation of all 71 security exploits) is performed by one of the paper's authors; independent expert review covers only a sample (12 scenarios, 6 generated), and the sampled expert evaluation reveals concern flags for 67% of non-CWE-400 exploits (at least one reviewer) and low agreement on exploit coverage, which somewhat tempers the 'same quality as experts' claim.

The CWE classification is only ~81% correct per expert evaluation, yet CWE labels are part of the benchmark output and used for aggregation/exclusion decisions; the paper acknowledges fundamental ambiguity but the benchmark's classification reliability remains a moderate open issue.

The benchmark is still modest in scale (40 scenarios, building on 28 existing ones), and difficulty control is partly achieved by coarse knobs (number of endpoints), so the claimed 'increasing difficulty' axis is only weakly validated.

Some tension between 'fully automatic generation' framing and the actual workflow, which includes ~15 minutes of human checking per scenario; this is honest but the framing in the abstract overstates the automation.

Presentation issues: several typos ('security tets', 'evaluation of evaluation of LLM-based code generation'), Figure 1/2 are dense and hard to parse, and some numbers (e.g., exploit false-negative concerns) are reported only qualitatively in the appendix rather than integrated into the headline claims.

The hard subset's low max scores (25% sec_pass@1 for the best model) may partly reflect exploit false negatives/generalization concerns flagged by experts, which could confound the difficulty narrative.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: manual expert benchmark creation for secure code generation does not scale, and the paper addresses contamination/difficulty scaling with an automated pipeline (AutoBaxBuilder) that generates scenarios, functional tests, and end-to-end exploits in the sound BaxBench execution-based framework.

Strong validation methodology: generated tests/exploits are compared against human-expert artifacts on the same BaxBench scenarios, with confusion matrices, per-scenario correlations, and reproduction of model rankings; the pipeline even surfaced and corrected two incorrect functional tests in the original BaxBench.

Thorough human evaluation: four security experts independently assess scenario realism, functional test correctness, and exploit soundness/CWE classification (Table 4), and the authors transparently discuss weak spots (CWE-400 unsoundness, 81% CWE correctness, low coverage agreement).

Honest failure-mode analysis (App. B.2), a CWE-400 ablation (App. A.6), and a self-generation bias ablation showing mild inflation for the orchestration model's own family; public release of AutoBaxBench with three difficulty tiers and low generation cost (~USD 4/scenario).
weaknesses: Contribution is largely incremental: the pipeline, scenario format, evaluation harness, and metrics are inherited from BaxBench; the novelty is the automated generation loop, which is an agentic engineering effort rather than a methodological advance.

Validation against expert-written tests uses BaxBench as 'ground truth' while simultaneously finding BaxBench tests to be wrong, which muddies the agreement metrics; ground-truth assumptions for sec_pass@1 agreement are similarly circular.

Benchmark scale is modest (40 scenarios, 10-20 per split) and scenario diversity is constrained by the fixed CWE list and prompt templates; many new scenarios appear formulaic (e.g., several mail-merge/forge variants in Table 3).

Dependence on a single orchestration LLM (GPT-5) raises concerns about generated-test distribution being tied to one model's biases; the bias ablation is very small (4 scenarios) and shows notable self-generation inflation (Claude 4.5: 95.2% vs 80.8% pass@1).

Some quantitative claims are weakened by internal inconsistencies: 17 spurious CWE-400 exploits are acknowledged, and 'only one unsound exploit of 71' (Sec. 4.2) sits awkwardly beside expert findings that all 4 inspected CWE-400 exploits raise concerns and coverage is rated at only 71%.

Reproducibility concerns: results depend on proprietary APIs (GPT-5, Claude 4.5, Grok 4) that drift over time, and the framework implementation/code release status is not clearly stated beyond the scenario release; typos and a missing URL in the contributions list indicate insufficient polish.

The claim of a 'guaranteed upper bound' on security rests on the soundness of the generated exploits; while the expert study supports mostly sound exploits, the 3.23% potential error margin and CWE misclassification (81% correct) mean the bound is softer than the framing suggests.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely problem: benchmarks for LLM code security suffer from contamination and require substantial manual effort to extend. An automated pipeline for bootstrapping scenario/test/exploit triplets in the BaxBench format is a useful contribution to the community.

Validation is unusually thorough for a benchmark-generation paper: (i) pipeline outputs are compared against human-expert artifacts on the same BaxBench scenarios, with confusion matrices on both pass@1 (83.5% agreement, precision 81.6%, recall 81.1%) and sec_pass@1; (ii) a structured expert study with 4 security experts on 12 scenarios reports average scores and inter-rater agreement (Table 4); (iii) an ablation replaces the orchestration/solution LLMs and checks for generation bias; (iv) a CWE-400 ablation quantifies the effect of including the weakest exploit class.

The paper is commendably honest about limitations: it reports that the generating model (Claude-4.5 Sonnet) scores substantially higher on self-generated scenarios (95.2% vs 80.8% pass@1), that CWE-400 exploits are unreliable (and excludes them with an ablation), that only 81% of CWE classifications are judged correct, and that exploit coverage is rated only 71%. It even documents pipeline failure modes (B.2) and reports two incorrect tests found in BaxBench itself.

Reproducibility support is strong: algorithms, per-step prompts (App. C), token/cost breakdowns, per-scenario statistics, and a released benchmark of 40 novel scenarios across three difficulty tiers, at a very low per-scenario cost (~USD 4).

The demonstration that the method finds exploits missed by human experts (e.g., OS Injection in FileSearch) with concrete evidence in App. A.4 is a convincing qualitative illustration that the approach can exceed expert-written tests, not merely match them.
weaknesses: Several central claims rest on partially single-annotator evidence. The '71 security exploits, only one unsound' finding and the 'same quality, if not more comprehensive' claim lean on manual annotation by one author, with the follow-up expert study limited to a sample of 6 scenarios (later 12 in App. A.5). Independent multi-annotator verification of all generated tasks would be needed to fully support the claim of matching expert-written tests.

The demonstrated generation bias is material: Claude-4.5 Sonnet performs 14+ points better on its self-generated benchmark than on the GPT-5-generated one, for both pass@1 and sec_pass@1. The ablation is small (3-4 scenarios), so the magnitude and generality of this bias for future users of the pipeline (who will likely use whatever frontier model is available) is under-characterized. This weakens the claim that automatically generated benchmarks are neutral evaluation instruments.

The validation against BaxBench treats BaxBench as ground truth while simultaneously finding two of its functional tests wrong and one specification ambiguous; the 16.5% disagreement on pass@1 is explained, but the correction of BaxBench tests by the authors of this paper introduces a circularity risk in the comparative evaluation. No third-party adjudication is reported.

The security-side soundness story ('no false positives, sound upper bound') is complicated by the paper's own findings: experts raised false-positive concerns for some non-CWE-400 exploits, CWE classification is only 81% correct, and coverage is rated low with very poor inter-rater agreement (22.58%). sec_pass@1 numbers should therefore be interpreted cautiously, which the paper acknowledges but does not fully resolve.

The novel benchmark is modest in scale (40 scenarios; the HARD split is only 10) and generated with a single orchestration model, so conclusions about difficulty scaling and subset construction from such a small sample have limited statistical support.

Originality is moderate: the technical core is a careful agentic refinement pipeline (execution-feedback iteration, hardened/weakened solution regularization, judge-based verdicts) built from known techniques (self-debugging, self-criticism, LLM-as-judge). The novelty lies in the application domain and validation rather than in a new method.

Presentation has notable blemishes that reduce polish: typos ('security tets', 'sustained security evaluation of evaluation of LLM-based code generation'), duplicated SWT-bench references (2024a/2024b), a release URL left blank ('release the scenarios at .'), and Figure 2/25/24 captions that appear copy-pasted or mismatched (Figures 24 and 25 captions are identical despite showing different content).

strengths: Addresses a genuine, important problem: scaling security benchmarks for LLM code generation beyond expert-written tasks (BaxBench), enabling contamination-free, tunable-difficulty evaluation.

Strong validation methodology: the pipeline's generated functional tests and exploits are compared against expert-written BaxBench artifacts (80.9% agreement on functional outcomes; 164/2227 false negatives on security), and all 71 generated exploits for BaxBench scenarios were manually audited, finding only one unsound exploit.

Comprehensive evaluation design: 14 frameworks across 6 languages, 16 models from 8 families, three difficulty splits, framework ablation, agentic-harness ablation, and a disjoint-model ablation to assess whether generating models are biased toward their own benchmark (Spearman rho > 0.9; no systematic bias found).

Honest and thorough failure analysis: false-negative taxonomy (73% genuinely missed, mostly CWE-522 plaintext password checks), documented failure modes (exploit overfitting to reference solutions, false positives from specification ambiguity), and transparent discussion of low inter-rater agreement on coverage judgements.

Clear practical contribution: ~12x reduction in human effort (3 hours to 15 minutes per scenario), <$4 API cost per scenario, 40 new scenarios more than doubling BaxBench; the discovery of genuine errors in BaxBench itself (incorrect MIME tests, ImageIO duration unit bug) is a valuable by-product.
Well-organized paper with detailed algorithms, prompts, and case studies in the appendix that make the pipeline methodology transparent and reproducible.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty relative to BaxBench: the core contribution is automating artifact generation for an existing benchmark design, using a fairly standard agentic generate-refine loop with execution feedback; the conceptual contribution is limited to this setting.

Heavy reliance on GPT-5 as the sole orchestration model for the main benchmark; while the ablation with Gemini 3 Pro shows robust rankings, benchmark quality (especially exploit sophistication and scenario difficulty) is inherently coupled to one frontier model's capabilities, and the pipeline's ceiling for very subtle vulnerabilities is not explored.

The human audit has limitations acknowledged by the authors: 12 sampled scenarios, low inter-rater agreement on exploit coverage (22.58%) and scenario ambiguity (50%), and the systematic A.6 annotation was performed by a single author. Coverage scored only 71%, so exploit generalizability to unseen implementations remains somewhat uncertain.

The exclusion of CWE-400 from headline results, while well-justified, is an asymmetry applied to a class where the automated pipeline underperforms; the defense that BaxBench's own CWE-400 exploits are also spurious is reasonable but reduces comparability with the original benchmark's full setup.

Some evaluation circularity risks remain: pipeline solution LLMs are excluded from the headline comparison, but the reference solutions used to validate tests/exploits come from the same generation LLMs, and scenario specifications are themselves LLM-generated, so specification ambiguity (79% unambiguous) propagates into all downstream judgments.

The released benchmark is by default anchored to Python-FastAPI reference solutions; the framework ablation mitigates this concern but the benchmark design is narrower than BaxBench's multi-framework references.
The code/benchmark release URL appears incomplete in the manuscript footnote, so reproducibility claims cannot be fully verified from the manuscript itself.

Difficulty tuning by endpoint count is a crude proxy for task difficulty; the EASY/MEDIUM/HARD splits conflate specification length and implementation complexity with the actual security reasoning difficulty.

strengths: Addresses a real and important problem: benchmark longevity for LLM code security evaluation. The motivation (contamination, difficulty scaling, cost of expert-written exploits) is well-grounded in the BaxBench line of work, and the proposed automation directly targets a documented bottleneck.

Unusually thorough validation for a benchmark-generation paper. The pipeline is validated against the expert-written BaxBench artifacts on the same 28 scenarios: high functional-test agreement (80.9%, confusion matrix in Fig. 5), a manual audit of all 71 generated exploits finding only one unsound case, and a systematic expert evaluation (Table 7) with inter-rater agreement reported. The finding that the pipeline discovered two incorrect functional tests and missed vulnerabilities in the original BaxBench is credible evidence of added value rather than mere replication.

Careful treatment of potential confounds: reference-framework ablation (Table 2-3), disjoint-model ablation with Spearman ρ > 0.9 (Fig. 8), a calibrated bias analysis for contamination-by-generation, and agentic-harness experiments (Table 4). The contamination-through-generation analysis with a neutral control group is a thoughtful addition rarely seen in LLM-generated benchmark papers.

Reproducibility: code and the 40-scenario benchmark are publicly released; costs and construction time are reported per scenario; prompts and algorithms are given in full in the appendix, including honest failure-mode case studies (App. B.2).

Honest limitations discussion: the authors flag low inter-rater agreement on exploit-coverage judgments, CWE-400 unsoundness, CWE-522 false negatives (plaintext password probing), and sample coverage of the human audit, and they quantify the ceiling that soundness (96.77%) imposes on sec_pass@1.
weaknesses: The contribution is incremental in framing: it automates benchmark construction following an existing benchmark's design (BaxBench) rather than introducing a new evaluation paradigm. The core method is a fairly conventional agentic generate-execute-refine loop; the novelty rests on the exploit generation with contrastive solutions (Fig. 3/Alg. 7) and the validation methodology.

The main pipeline uses Python-FastAPI as the only reference framework for constructing AutoBaxBench scenarios; while the Fastify/Go-Gin ablation (Table 2) supports robustness, the released benchmark itself was built from a single reference language, which may bake in Python-specific assumptions for the new 40 scenarios.

Expert evaluation of the newly generated AutoBaxBench scenarios covers only 6 of 40 scenarios, and several metrics show low inter-rater agreement (e.g., 22.58% on exploit coverage, 50% on scenario ambiguity/realism). The soundness claims for the new benchmark are therefore weaker than for the BaxBench-validation subset.

Exclusion of CWE-400 from the main results is a post-hoc filtering decision. It is justified by manual analysis and ablated (App. A.8), but a cleaner solution (e.g., tightening the exploit criteria) would have been preferable; it also reveals a systematic weakness of the pipeline (DoS-by-load rather than amplification-based exploits).

Evaluation of evaluated models is uneven: reasoning models are sampled only once at temperature 0 while non-reasoning models get 3 samples at 0.4, which weakens direct score comparisons across model classes. Additionally, the LLM-as-judge steps that decide exploit TP/TN during refinement introduce potential circularity, partially mitigated but not fully eliminated by the human audits.

The 12× human-effort-reduction figure is based on a coarse 3-hour-per-scenario estimate for manual construction; a more careful task decomposition or time-tracking study would strengthen this headline claim.

strengths: Well-motivated and practical contribution: automating construction of end-to-end security exploits and functional tests addresses a genuine scalability/longevity problem for benchmarks like BaxBench (contamination, rising difficulty, expert cost), and the reported ~12x reduction in human effort and <$4/scenario cost is a concrete, verifiable claim.

The validation methodology is unusually thorough and multi-pronged: (i) running both expert-written and pipeline-generated test/exploit suites on the same LLM-generated solutions (Figures 4-5), (ii) confusion-matrix agreement analysis, (iii) a full manual audit of all 71 generated exploits with only one unsound exploit found, (iv) a structured expert evaluation (Table 7) reporting both average scores and inter-rater agreement, and (v) a detailed false-negative analysis (Figure 11).

Careful contamination controls: the validation uses a knowledge cutoff predating BaxBench's release and disabled web search; the disjoint-model ablation (Section 4.4, A.4) with a neutral control group and calibration analysis convincingly shows no generator-model self-bias, and Spearman correlations >0.9 support robustness of the evaluation signal.

Honest and detailed treatment of weaknesses: the paper reports where it falls short of BaxBench (164 missed insecure solutions, CWE-522 plaintext-password probing), documents concrete failure modes (Appendix B.2, e.g., exploit overfitting to reference solutions), discusses low inter-rater agreement on coverage judgments, and even discovered and reported errors in the original BaxBench (A.5), which strengthens credibility.

The generated benchmark (40 scenarios, three difficulty splits, 11 CWEs) plus evaluation of 10+ models across 14 frameworks is a substantive, publicly released artifact, and the agentic-harness and reference-framework ablations (A.2, A.3) further de-risk design choices.
weaknesses: Moderate functional test agreement (80.9%) is only partially explained: the paper attributes disagreements to two erroneous and two ambiguous BaxBench cases, but with only four outlier scenarios analyzed in depth, residual uncertainty about whether some generated tests are over- or under-strict remains, which could bias pass@1 on the new benchmark.

CWE-400 is excluded from all main-paper results due to unreliable generated exploits; although ablated in A.8 and honestly motivated, this is a post-hoc filtering decision made by the same pipeline authors, and a fully automatic pipeline that still requires this class of manual curation slightly weakens the 'minimal human intervention' claim.

Exploit generalization is a real concern acknowledged by the authors: expert evaluation rates only 71% of exploits as having high coverage with very low inter-rater agreement (22.58%), and failure modes show exploits overfitting to reference solutions (e.g., the /uploads endpoint in FrameExtract). The argument that this only underestimates sec_pass@1 is plausible but not fully quantified for the new 40 scenarios.

Pipeline dependence on a single frontier orchestration LLM (GPT-5) makes the method's cost/quality profile contingent on one closed model; the ablated benchmark uses Gemini 3 Pro, but per-step sensitivity to orchestrator capability (e.g., with weaker open models) is not characterized.

Difficulty is operationalized almost entirely by endpoint count, a crude proxy; and some low-resource model scores (e.g., Qwen2.5 7B near 0 on harder splits, Login scenario with only n=3 solutions) raise questions about statistical stability of fine-grained numbers, though aggregate trends are consistent.
